paragraphs: Recognizing an object and estimating its pose place different demands on an image representation. Category recognition should remain stable as the viewpoint changes, while pose estimation needs to preserve information about those changes. This paper studies how convolutional neural networks can support both tasks together, making that tension central to the analysis.

The authors adapt and compare several CNN architectures for simultaneous categorization and pose estimation. They examine the representations within different layers to understand how pose information is retained and how it interacts with category information. This makes the investigation about both model performance and the internal representations that support the two predictions.

Experiments on two large multiview datasets report performance beyond the previous state of the art. The contribution combines an empirical comparison with an investigation of where the two tasks impose competing requirements. Its practical significance is that designing a joint model requires attention to which variations its representations preserve, as well as which variations they suppress.
icml-2016-a-comparative-analysis-and-stu.tldr: The paper compares CNN architectures and their internal representations for jointly recognizing object categories and estimating pose.

paragraphs: CF-NADE is a neural autoregressive model for collaborative filtering, where observed preferences help predict other preferences. The architecture draws inspiration from restricted Boltzmann machine approaches to recommendation and neural autoregressive distribution estimation. The paper develops a basic model and then examines several ways to improve its predictions and scalability.

One modification shares parameters across different rating values, connecting parts of the model that would otherwise be treated separately. Another uses a factored representation to improve scalability. The authors also introduce a training cost that respects the ordering of preferences: rating levels carry an ordered relationship, rather than simply identifying unrelated categories. This ordinal cost produces superior performance in their experiments.

The reported single-hidden-layer model outperforms previous state-of-the-art methods on MovieLens 1M, MovieLens 10M, and Netflix. Additional hidden layers can further improve performance, with only a moderate increase in computational complexity. Together, these findings support both the basic autoregressive approach and the value of adapting its parameterization and training objective to the structure of ratings.
icml-2016-a-neural-autoregressive-approa.tldr: CF-NADE combines neural autoregressive modeling, rating-aware training, and scalable parameterizations to improve collaborative filtering.

paragraphs: Domain adaptation asks how learning from one distribution can support predictions on another. This paper studies the problem for majority-vote models, which combine the decisions of multiple classifiers. The goal is to use information from a source domain to construct a vote that performs well on the target domain.

The main contribution is an upper bound on target risk that connects a source-domain error measure with disagreement among voters on target examples. A ratio-based measure of distributional divergence controls the trade-off between those quantities. The bound suggests concentrating on regions where source data provides useful information, linking the relevance of source observations to the target prediction problem.

The authors turn this relationship into a PAC-Bayesian generalization bound, specialize the theory to linear classifiers, and derive a learning algorithm. They also conduct experiments on real data. The resulting contribution links a theoretical account of transfer with a concrete learning procedure: source accuracy, target disagreement, and distributional differences are considered together when constructing the model.
icml-2016-a-new-pac-bayesian-perspective.tldr: A PAC-Bayesian bound connects target-domain risk to source error, voter disagreement, and distributional divergence, yielding a learning algorithm.

paragraphs: Classification error gives a direct measure of a neural network's predictions, but the authors seek an additional way to assess its learned weights. Their question includes comparisons between networks with different architectures. The paper introduces the Extended Data Jacobian Matrix as a tool for analyzing properties of these differently structured networks.

The analysis focuses on the matrix's spectrum, a collection of numerical characteristics that summarizes aspects of the matrix. The authors find that this spectrum strongly distinguishes networks with different structures and performance. This supplies an additional perspective on learned networks, connecting an internal mathematical description with differences observed in their predictive behavior.

The authors then use that observation to design a regularization method. They report improvements in network performance comparable to those obtained with dropout, interpreting this result as support for the spectral observation. The work therefore moves from analyzing trained weights to using that analysis during learning. Its stated evidence concerns the discriminating value of the spectrum and the effectiveness of the resulting regularizer.
icml-2016-analysis-of-deep-neural-networ.tldr: The Extended Data Jacobian Matrix provides a spectral view of learned networks and motivates a regularizer with improvements comparable to dropout.

paragraphs: Variational Bayesian inference makes difficult posterior calculations manageable by approximating a distribution with simpler factors. A key design choice is how latent variables are grouped: each group can be updated while the others remain fixed. This paper examines how that choice affects methods seeking sparse or low-rank explanations of high-dimensional observations.

The authors compare two popular constructions, based on Gaussian scale mixture priors and bilinear Gaussian priors. Both can encourage sparsity or low rank, depending on the setting. By rewriting their variational objectives, the paper makes their behavior easier to analyze and compares local-minimum avoidance, sensitivity to feature transformations and correlations, and computational complexity.

The purpose is to explain why different variational factorizations behave differently and help determine which is advantageous in a particular setting. This is relevant across the structured estimation applications discussed in the abstract, including matrix completion and robust principal component analysis. The authors also suggest that the principles may extend to other structured inverse problems, presenting that broader relevance as a prospect.
icml-2016-analysis-of-variational-bayesi.tldr: The paper analyzes two common variational Bayesian factorizations to explain their trade-offs in sparse and low-rank estimation.

paragraphs: This paper applies Bayesian optimization to finding the lowest point on a potential energy surface. The application concerns interactions between molecules and surfaces, which matter in settings such as environmental catalysis and gas sensing. The proposed Bayesian Active Site Calculator, or BASC, aims to make this search both rapid and accurate.

BASC includes a schedule for balancing exploration with exploitation: searching less understood possibilities while also investigating promising ones. It also uses a custom covariance kernel that represents properties of the objective function. These choices adapt the optimization procedure to the energy-search problem, incorporating information about the objective into how the search is organized.

The authors test BASC on carbon monoxide adsorption on a hematite substrate, considering cases with and without a defect. In those trials, it outperforms differential evolution and constrained minima hopping, the two comparison approaches named in the abstract. The findings support the usefulness of tailored Bayesian optimization for these examples of molecule-surface interaction, with the reported comparison tied to those trial settings.
icml-2016-basc-applying-bayesian-optimiz.tldr: BASC tailors Bayesian optimization to potential energy searches and outperforms two established methods in carbon monoxide adsorption trials.

paragraphs: Correlation clustering groups vertices using positive and negative labels on their connecting edges. A positive edge counts as an error when its endpoints are separated, and a negative edge counts as an error when they are grouped together. The usual objective adds all such mistakes across the graph into one total.

This paper introduces objectives that depend more generally on the number of errors at each vertex. For example, an objective can focus on the vertex experiencing the most mistakes. This changes which aspects of a clustering matter: two partitions with similar total errors can distribute those errors very differently among their vertices.

The authors provide a rounding algorithm that converts fractional clusterings into discrete partitions while increasing each vertex's error count by only a constant factor. Because the guarantee operates locally at every vertex, it supports constant-factor approximation algorithms for a wide variety of objectives. The central contribution is therefore a rounding guarantee flexible enough to preserve multiple ways of evaluating local clustering errors.
icml-2016-correlation-clustering-and-bic.tldr: A rounding algorithm controls clustering errors at each vertex, enabling constant-factor approximations for many locally sensitive objectives.

paragraphs: The paper develops a nonparametric extension of tensor regression, allowing nonlinear relationships in a high-dimensional tensor space. Its organizing idea is to break a complicated relationship into simpler local functions. Low-rank tensor decomposition supplies the structure for that breakdown, connecting the representation of the tensor with the representation of the nonlinear function.

The authors show that their formulation can substantially improve the convergence rate of estimation relative to naive nonparametric approaches. Under specific conditions, it also retains consistency for the same function class. These claims concern both how quickly estimation improves and whether it approaches the intended function, with the stated conditions governing the comparison.

To estimate the local functions, the paper develops a Bayesian estimator using a Gaussian process prior. Experiments support the theoretical properties and show strong performance when predicting a summary statistic of a real complex network. The approach matters because it connects flexible nonlinear estimation with a structured decomposition, using simpler component functions to address an otherwise high-dimensional regression problem.
icml-2016-doubly-decomposing-nonparametr.tldr: Low-rank decomposition breaks nonlinear tensor regression into local functions, improving estimation rates under specified conditions.

paragraphs: Vector autoregressive models describe relationships in multivariate time-dependent data. Estimating structured versions raises a difficulty absent from independent-sample analyses: observations and covariates can be strongly dependent. This paper studies that setting with correlated noise, allowing model structure to be expressed through a suitable norm rather than restricting attention to one particular penalty.

The authors establish finite-sample bounds on the error in estimated VAR parameters. Within their analysis, the error has the same order as that of the corresponding Lasso-type estimator using independent samples. The framework covers any norm, with Lasso, group Lasso, and order weighted Lasso given as examples of the structures it accommodates.

The proof combines generic chaining, sub-exponential martingale results, and spectral representations of VAR models to handle the dependence. Experiments on synthetic and real data examine several structures and support the theory. The stated result shows that dependence can be addressed explicitly while retaining the estimation-error order associated with corresponding independent-data methods in the analyzed setting.
icml-2016-estimating-structured-vector-a.tldr: The paper bounds structured VAR estimation error with dependent data, matching the order of corresponding independent-sample estimators.

paragraphs: In sequential prediction, the expected signal and the variability around it can both change with explanatory variables. This is the heteroscedastic setting studied in the paper. A prediction method must therefore address variation in the signal alongside variation in its uncertainty, rather than treating the noise level as fixed throughout the sequence.

The authors use regret minimization to construct an efficient online learning algorithm. Their approach does not require error terms to follow a specified distribution. This makes the distributional treatment a central feature of the contribution: the algorithm addresses changing variance without building the method around a particular assumed shape for the errors.

The algorithm can also be adjusted to supply confidence bounds for predictions. The paper presents an application to ARCH models and an empirical study that supports the theoretical results. Together, these contributions connect sequential prediction, variable uncertainty, and regret-based learning. The confidence-bound extension adds an uncertainty description to the predictions produced by the online procedure.
icml-2016-heteroscedastic-sequences-beyo.tldr: An online prediction algorithm handles input-dependent signal and variance without prescribing an error distribution.

paragraphs: Hyperparameters influence model complexity, so choosing them affects both predictive accuracy and the computational effort spent on training. This paper proposes an algorithm for optimizing continuous hyperparameters using approximate gradient information. Its key practical feature is that hyperparameter updates can occur before the model's own parameters have fully converged.

Allowing inexact gradients changes how model fitting and hyperparameter selection can be coordinated. Instead of requiring a fully converged fit before every update, the method can work with intermediate information. The authors provide sufficient conditions for global convergence of the procedure, involving regularity of the relevant functions and summability of the approximation errors.

The experiments tune regularization constants for L2-regularized logistic regression and kernel ridge regression. The reported benchmarks find the approach highly competitive with state-of-the-art methods. The contribution thus combines a way to update hyperparameters during incomplete training with theory describing when controlled approximation errors are compatible with convergence. The stated guarantees depend on those conditions, rather than allowing arbitrary gradient inaccuracies.
icml-2016-hyperparameter-optimization-wi.tldr: Approximate gradients allow continuous hyperparameters to be updated before model fitting converges, with convergence guaranteed under sufficient conditions.

paragraphs: The paper shows that empirical risk for most familiar loss functions can be separated into a linear label-dependent term and a label-free term. The label-dependent part is summarized by a mean operator, which acts as a sufficient statistic for the labels in this formulation. The result includes nonsmooth and nonconvex losses and applies in any reproducing kernel Hilbert space.

This factorization gives weak supervision a concrete point of entry into learning. Once the mean operator has been estimated, algorithms such as stochastic gradient descent and proximal methods can be adapted with little additional change. The same analysis also tightens existing generalization bounds and offers a different interpretation of what those bounds capture.

The authors apply the approach to asymmetric label noise, connecting and extending earlier work. They show that most losses have a form of noise robustness that depends on the data through the mean operator. That qualification is central: the result identifies a data-dependent source of robustness rather than asserting that every loss withstands every pattern of corrupted labels.
icml-2016-loss-factorization-weakly-supe.tldr: Factoring empirical risk through a label mean operator enables weak-supervision adaptations and reveals data-dependent robustness to label noise.

paragraphs: Average training loss summarizes performance across examples, whereas maximal loss focuses on the example with the largest loss. The paper examines why and how to optimize this latter objective. It addresses three concerns: compatibility with online learning, whether improving training accuracy helps on unseen examples, and sensitivity to outliers.

The authors describe and analyze a procedure that converts any online algorithm into a maximal-loss minimizer. This connects a worst-example objective with algorithms that process only a few examples per iteration. The construction addresses the computational appeal commonly associated with average-loss training by making online algorithms available for the maximal-loss objective as well.

The paper also provides theoretical and empirical evidence that, in some situations, better training accuracy is crucial for good performance on unseen data. It proposes robust variants to handle outliers, addressing a stated weakness of maximal-loss training. These results support considering the objective when the situation warrants it, while preserving the paper's qualified claim about when improved training performance benefits generalization.
icml-2016-minimizing-the-maximal-loss-ho.tldr: The paper converts online algorithms into maximal-loss minimizers and shows why this objective can improve generalization in some situations.

paragraphs: The paper studies alternating Gibbs sampling, a modification of the classical Gibbs sampling procedure. Its defining feature is that several variables are sampled together from their joint conditional distribution. The unit of an update is therefore a collection of variables, with their joint conditional relationship retained during that update.

The central question is the sampler's mixing rate: how quickly the sampling process approaches the distribution it is intended to represent. This places the emphasis on the behavior of repeated sampling updates. Describing which conditional distribution to sample from specifies the update rule; studying mixing asks how that rule behaves as the process continues.

The investigation gives particular attention to restricted Boltzmann machines and related models. Within that focus, the contribution is an analysis of convergence behavior for a sampling procedure that updates multiple variables simultaneously. The abstract identifies the algorithmic mechanism and the quantity being investigated, so the supported takeaway is the study of mixing rates in these models, without a stated direction or magnitude of improvement.
icml-2016-mixing-rates-for-the-alternati.tldr: The paper investigates how quickly alternating Gibbs sampling mixes, focusing on restricted Boltzmann machines and related models.

paragraphs: The paper studies first-order optimization methods whose step-size schedules do not adapt to the particular objective, except through limited information such as smoothness and strong convexity parameters. It calls these algorithms oblivious. The question is how few iterations methods in this class can require to achieve a given accuracy.

The authors establish lower bounds for smooth convex and smooth strongly convex objectives when the relevant parameters are known. These bounds hold independently of dimension, strengthening the corresponding traditional oracle-model bounds in that respect. The analysis uses a structure-based framework, making the form of the algorithm central to the impossibility results.

The paper also examines what can be achieved without knowledge of the strong convexity parameter. It uses this analysis to formalize a restriction on methods with time-invariant step sizes: their iteration complexity for smooth convex functions must be at least proportional to L/ε. The findings clarify how algorithm structure, parameter knowledge, and step-size scheduling constrain attainable convergence speed.
icml-2016-on-the-iteration-complexity-of.tldr: Dimension-independent lower bounds reveal how fixed scheduling rules and limited parameter knowledge constrain first-order optimization.

paragraphs: Training neural networks involves a nonconvex objective, creating a gap between practical success and worst-case computational difficulty. This paper examines the geometry of that objective for ReLU networks initialized randomly. It asks whether the starting location already lies in a region with favorable possibilities for reducing the training objective.

The authors identify conditions giving a high probability of starting at a point connected to a global minimum by a monotonically decreasing path. They also identify conditions giving a high probability of starting in a suitably defined basin whose minimum objective value is small. These are related but distinct geometric properties of the initialization and its surrounding region.

A recurring finding is that larger, overspecified networks are more likely to possess these favorable properties. This supports a geometric explanation for why additional network capacity can help optimization. The claims concern the existence of descending paths and the quality of basins under stated conditions; they do not equate those properties with a guarantee that a particular training algorithm follows such a path.
icml-2016-on-the-quality-of-the-initial-.tldr: Under identified conditions, larger ReLU networks are more likely to initialize in geometrically favorable regions of the training objective.

paragraphs: Feedback graphs describe which losses a learner can observe after taking an action. This paper studies online learning when those graphs can change each round and are never fully disclosed. The learner receives feedback without complete knowledge of the structure governing which observations become available.

The authors prove a sharp distinction between adversarial and stochastic settings. In the adversarial case, even dense graphs cannot improve the guaranteed regret beyond the trivial bound obtained by using only the learner's own loss. In the stochastic case, their algorithm achieves regret of order √(αT), up to logarithmic factors, when every hidden graph has independence number at most α.

The paper also considers a more general setting where an action need not reveal its own loss. There, hiding the graph can make learning impossible even in simple cases. These results show that the usefulness of additional feedback depends on both the process generating losses and knowledge of the observation structure, rather than solely on how many observations might be available.
icml-2016-online-learning-with-feedback-.tldr: Hidden feedback graphs permit strong stochastic regret guarantees but can eliminate the benefits of extra feedback in adversarial settings.

paragraphs: Probabilistic finite automata model distributions over finite symbol sequences using latent variables. They are commonly learned through iterative likelihood-improvement methods such as expectation-maximization. Method-of-moments approaches offer a much faster alternative with PAC-style guarantees, but earlier versions have an important drawback: the learned automaton may fail to define a proper probability distribution.

This paper proposes a method-of-moments algorithm that retains PAC-style guarantees while producing automata that define proper distributions. The distinction matters because a statistical learning guarantee alone does not ensure that an output can be used as a valid probabilistic model. The abstract also identifies invalid distributions as an obstacle to initializing iterative learning algorithms.

The authors evaluate their method on synthetic problems from the PAutomaC challenge and real datasets drawn from Wikipedia. Comparisons include previous method-of-moments algorithms and expectation-maximization. The central stated contribution is the combination of probabilistically valid outputs with formal learning guarantees, addressing a concrete applicability problem in earlier moment-based approaches.
icml-2016-pac-learning-of-probabilistic-.tldr: A new method-of-moments algorithm learns probabilistic automata that define valid distributions while retaining PAC-style guarantees.

paragraphs: The Max K-Armed Bandit problem treats each sampled reward as the value of a separate item. The learner chooses among several stochastic sources and seeks an item with the highest possible value. Each source produces independent, identically distributed rewards from an unknown distribution, so choosing where to sample is part of the search.

The paper assumes a known lower bound on the reward distributions' tail functions. Under this assumption, the authors derive a lower bound on the number of samples required by any algorithm satisfying the specified accuracy and confidence requirements. They then propose an algorithm that reaches this bound up to logarithmic factors.

This connects an information requirement with an achievable sampling procedure, showing near-matching sample complexity within the stated framework. The authors also analyze robustness to the modeling assumptions and compare the algorithm with a non-adaptive procedure that selects arms randomly. Those analyses examine both the role of the tail assumption and the consequences of adapting source selection during the search.
icml-2016-pac-lower-bounds-and-efficient.tldr: Under a known tail lower bound, a Max K-Armed Bandit algorithm matches the sample-complexity lower bound up to logarithmic factors.

paragraphs: Polynomial networks and factorization machines both model feature interactions for classification and regression. Such interactions allow predictions to depend on combinations of input features. This paper places the two model families in a common framework, using that shared perspective to investigate their properties and develop efficient training methods.

The central reformulation casts parameter learning as the estimation of a low-rank symmetric tensor. This gives both models a shared mathematical object through which their parameters and interactions can be studied. The authors solve the resulting estimation problem using multi-convex optimization, connecting the unified representation directly to the construction of training algorithms.

The approach is demonstrated on regression and recommender-system tasks. Its contribution is therefore both conceptual and computational: it provides a way to reason about two models together and uses that understanding to design learning procedures. The stated demonstrations establish the application settings, while the abstract's main methodological claim is the value of low-rank tensor estimation as a common view of parameter learning.
icml-2016-polynomial-networks-and-factor.tldr: A low-rank symmetric tensor formulation unifies polynomial networks and factorization machines and leads to efficient training algorithms.

paragraphs: An optimization method produces successive candidate solutions, but assessing their progress requires a meaningful measure of remaining error. This paper proposes an algorithm-independent framework for adding primal-dual certificates to existing methods. These certificates provide a way to diagnose optimization progress, with particular relevance to machine learning problems.

The framework supplies efficiently computable duality gaps and corresponding convergence-rate guarantees. The authors obtain new primal-dual rates for Lasso and many problems involving L1, Elastic Net, group Lasso, or total-variation regularization. More generally, the theory covers generalized linear models regularized by any norm, giving the approach a broad class of applications.

A stated feature is that the duality gaps are defined globally while the original optimization problem remains unchanged in the region of interest. This connects practical progress measurement with guarantees about how those measurements improve. Because the framework is algorithm-independent, its role is to equip optimization methods with certificates rather than requiring one specific solver for every covered problem.
icml-2016-primal-dual-rates-and-certific.tldr: An algorithm-independent framework gives norm-regularized learning problems computable primal-dual certificates and convergence rates.

paragraphs: Stochastic Dual Coordinate Ascent is commonly used to minimize regularized objectives built from convex losses. This paper describes variants that broaden that setting in several ways. The methods do not rely on duality and do not require an explicit regularization term, changing two features associated with the usual SDCA formulation.

The analysis also allows individual loss functions to be nonconvex. The crucial condition is that their expected loss remains strongly convex. This separates the shape of each component from the shape of the combined objective: unfavorable curvature in individual losses is compatible with the aggregate property required by the result.

Under that condition, the authors prove linear convergence rates, meaning that the convergence guarantee has a geometric rate. The result broadens the applicability of SDCA-style methods while keeping strong convexity at the expected-loss level central to the theory. Its significance lies in identifying which familiar ingredients can be removed without losing the stated rate, and which aggregate property still supports the guarantee.
icml-2016-sdca-without-duality-regulariz.tldr: SDCA variants achieve linear convergence without duality or explicit regularization when the expected loss is strongly convex, even with nonconvex components.

paragraphs: The paper addresses large-scale nonconvex optimization with cardinality constraints. These constraints restrict how many components of a solution can be nonzero, making sparsity an explicit requirement of the optimization problem. The authors propose a stochastic variance-reduced algorithm for a class of problems with this structure.

The theoretical contribution gives sufficient conditions under which the algorithm has strong linear convergence guarantees and optimal estimation accuracy in high dimensions. These concern two different aspects of the solution: how quickly the optimization procedure converges and how accurately it estimates the desired parameters. Both claims are tied to the conditions established for the analyzed problem class.

Numerical experiments demonstrate efficiency in parameter estimation and computational performance. The paper therefore connects sparse solution requirements with a stochastic optimization approach and evaluates both statistical and computational behavior. Its stated findings support the method for the covered class of nonconvex sparse-learning problems, with the convergence and accuracy guarantees resting on sufficient conditions rather than on nonconvexity or sparsity alone.
icml-2016-stochastic-variance-reduced-op.tldr: A variance-reduced stochastic algorithm offers linear convergence and optimal high-dimensional estimation accuracy under sufficient conditions for sparse nonconvex problems.

paragraphs: Subspace clustering with missing data groups incomplete observations according to their underlying subspaces. The paper asks how much observed information is sufficient for this task. With ambient dimension d and subspace dimension r, earlier theory left a large gap between the stated necessary number of columns per subspace and the known sufficient number.

The authors close that gap by showing that O(rd) columns per subspace are sufficient, matching the necessary scale described in the abstract. They derive deterministic sampling conditions that specify information-theoretic requirements and distinguish sampling regimes. These conditions make the pattern of available information part of the analysis, alongside the number of columns.

The results also explain the performance of existing subspace-clustering methods. Beyond the sample requirements, the paper supplies a practical algorithm for deterministically certifying the output of any method for this problem. This connects a theoretical account of when the data contains enough information with a separate procedure for checking a proposed clustering result.
icml-2016-the-information-theoretic-requ.tldr: Deterministic sampling conditions close the sample-requirement gap for subspace clustering with missing data and enable output certification.

paragraphs: The paper studies how efficiently first-order methods can reach a stationary point of a nonconvex objective. A stationary point is the convergence target here, so the result concerns reaching a point with little remaining first-order change. The setting of particular interest is an objective expressed as a sum of smooth functions.

The authors adapt variance reduction from convex optimization and develop a new analysis suited to nonconvex problems. Their minibatch stochastic method achieves an O(1/ε) convergence rate, improving on the O(1/ε²) stochastic gradient rate described in the abstract. They also report a speed advantage over full gradient descent by a factor of Ω(n^(1/3)).

The significance is that stochastic updates can achieve the stated faster rate through variance reduction even in this nonconvex setting. The paper demonstrates the methods on empirical risk minimization with nonconvex losses and on neural-network training. These experiments accompany the theoretical advance, whose stated scope is efficient stationary-point convergence for objectives that are sums of smooth functions.
icml-2016-variance-reduction-for-faster-.tldr: Variance reduction accelerates stationary-point convergence for smooth finite-sum nonconvex objectives, with theory and learning experiments supporting the approach.
